title: Neuromancer, first edition
lede: William Gibson’s 1984 novel, published by Ace Books with a cover by James Warhola, which set the terms of cyberpunk: cyberspace, the matrix, and jacking in.
summary: The novel that defined cyberpunk and named cyberspace. William Gibson, Ace Books, 1984; cover by James Warhola.

creator.name: William Gibson (author); James Warhola (cover artist, first edition)

evidence.note: Based on the Wikipedia article, read as wikitext on 2026-10-02, whose infobox names James Warhola as the cover artist of the first edition. The cover image was not inspected, so this record makes no claim about its appearance.

styles.note: The genre’s defining novel. The style record dates the look from Blade Runner and Akira in 1982 and Neuromancer in 1984. It supplies the vocabulary of the terminal and HUD side of the style.

context: Wikipedia: *Neuromancer* was published by Ace Books on 1 July 1984, with a first-edition cover by James Warhola. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neuromancer).
It “remains the first and only novel to win all three of the Hugo Award, the Nebula Award for Best Novel, and the Philip K. Dick Award”. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neuromancer).
Wikipedia’s Cyberpunk article notes that the novel is set in Chiba, Japan, and that its influence “dominated the early cyberpunk movement”. [Cyberpunk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyberpunk).
interpretation: The book gives the style its ideas rather than its pictures: a city of data, terminals, and bodies wired into machines. Designers turn these into terminal type, data panels, and HUD frames.
Its Japanese setting links it to the same Tokyo and Hong Kong imagery as [Blade Runner](ref:blade-runner-1982) and [Akira](ref:akira-film-1988).
borrow: Name panels and controls with short technical terms and codes, as the novel names its systems.
